waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Road's-end trailhead on Cascade River Road (23.1 mi gravel from Marblemount); NPS wilderness permit required for camps beyond Cascade Pass.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead is at the very end of Cascade River Road (FR-15), about 23.1 miles of gravel road from Marblemount, at roughly 3,600 feet. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park here. Overnight parties also need a North Cascades backcountry camping permit for Kool-Aid Lake, picked up in person in Marblemount before you drive out.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Maintained trail tops out here; leave it for the unmaintained climber's path bearing SSE toward Cache Glacier.
waypoints.directions: The Cascade Pass Trail is well-graded and heavily switchbacked the whole way, 3.7 miles and about 1,700 ft to the notch between Mixup Peak and Cascade Peak. It melts out by early to mid summer and is the busiest stretch of the trip, since it is a popular day hike in its own right. Nothing here needs route-finding; the work starts at the pass.

waypoints.name: Cache Glacier toe / Mixup Peak traverse
waypoints.note: Rising traverse on snow or heather across Mixup Peak's east flank to the base of Cache Glacier; isolated crevasses and firm morning snow can require an axe.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the pass and pick up a climber's path bearing south-southeast, making a rising traverse across open heather and snow benches on Mixup Peak's east flank. The path is intermittent and vanishes entirely under early-season snow, so this is where navigation starts to matter. It brings you to the toe of the Cache Glacier around 6,000 ft, where firm morning snow makes an ice axe worth its weight.

waypoints.name: Cache Col
waypoints.note: Glaciated gap atop Cache Glacier between Magic Mountain and Mixup Peak; descend SSE from here toward Kool-Aid Lake.
waypoints.directions: Ascend the glacier on moderate snow, steepening to about 35 degrees near the top, to reach the col. This glacier is small and generally free of significant crevasse hazard, but it is still a snow slope with runout below, so crampons are worth carrying depending on season and how firm it is.

waypoints.name: Kool-Aid Lake
waypoints.note: Small tarn with established bivy sites used as base camp for the peak; outlet is snowbound and unreliable for water into early summer.
waypoints.directions: From the col the route drops rather than climbs: a climber's path makes a descending traverse to the southeast down to the lake. Do not continue north over the col. This is the last reliable water of the trip, and the outlet can still be snowbound into early summer, so fill here before going up.

waypoints.name: Magic Mountain–Hurry-up Peak col
waypoints.note: Climb roughly 1,000 ft from Kool-Aid Lake to this saddle, then gain Magic Mountain's south ridge toward the false summit.
waypoints.directions: From the lake the ground turns up again onto heather and scree leading east to the saddle between Magic Mountain and Hurry-Up Peak, where the South Ridge proper begins. There is no water at all above the lake, so leave camp carrying what you need. The slope is uniform and featureless in cloud, which is the only real navigational catch on this leg.

waypoints.name: Corkscrew ledges below false summit
waypoints.note: Past the false summit, drop about 80 ft down a loose gully to exposed Class 3-4 ledges that corkscrew the east side of the peak; a hand line or short belay is often used here.
waypoints.directions: Follow the South Ridge up on heather and rock at class 3 to a false summit, roughly 50 ft below and southeast of the true one. Do not try to stay on the crest from there. Drop about 50-80 ft down a loose, dirty gully on the far side to reach the ledge system, which is the technical crux of the whole outing.

waypoints.name: Magic Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit, marking the northern terminus of the Ptarmigan Traverse on the North Cascades NP / Glacier Peak Wilderness boundary.
waypoints.directions: The ledges are broken, exposed class 3-4 and corkscrew around the east side of the summit tower to the top. A hand line or a short belay is commonly used, and many parties rappel this section on the way down off a sling around a horn or chockstone, since there is no fixed hardware on this summit. Fresh snow can force a detour through the moat, and the loose rock means this section bites harder on the descent than on the way up.
